title: Nachiketa turns down the horses
hook: Death offers a boy horses, gold and a long life if he'll drop one question. he says keep them
carry: moksha isn't earned; it's what the self already is

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Maitreyi: scripture breathed out by a great being, and the way to know Brahman.

In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa watches his father give away old, worn-out cows at a great sacrifice. To whom will you give me? the boy asks, again and again, until his father snaps: to Death. So Nachiketa goes to the house of Yama, Death himself, and waits three nights without food. Yama, who has left a guest unfed, offers him three wishes. The third: when a person dies, some say they still are, some say they aren't. Teach me. Yama tries to change the subject. Take sons and grandsons who live a hundred years, cattle, elephants, gold, horses, wide lands, as long a life as you like. Nachiketa says: these last only until tomorrow. Keep your horses; keep your songs. And Yama, pleased, praises him: the good and the pleasant come to everyone; the wise choose the good, and you have.
screen: `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `HORSES, GOLD, A LONG LIFE.` → `KEEP THEM.`

segments.voice: Shankara makes the same point in his comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line, which says, in effect: but that, because the texts are connected in it. The small word but, he says, turns away an objection from the Mimamsa school, thinkers who take the Veda very seriously and hold that its sentences exist to tell people what to do. So, they say, the Upanishads must be about action too. Shankara answers: no, they teach Brahman, something that already is. His reason echoes Nachiketa. Anything produced by action has a beginning, and whatever begins also ends. If freedom, moksha, were made by action, it would end too. So moksha isn't produced, reached, changed or cleaned up. It's what the self already is, and knowing removes what hid it, the way a lamp shows a room it didn't build. Shankara isn't saying action is pointless; good action and devotion ready the mind. But the last step isn't a doing. Some other Vedanta schools see freedom as the Lord's gift to devotion. Today it's easy to treat even the spiritual life like a points system. Nachiketa waved the prizes away; this teaching says the deepest freedom was never a prize.
screen: `BUT: AN OBJECTION TURNED AWAY.` · `WHAT BEGINS ALSO ENDS.` · `MOKSHA IS NOT MADE.` · `FREEDOM WAS NEVER A PRIZE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two or three things you'll do today. As each one comes up, offer it in your heart without asking what it will earn; many Hindus do this with a short prayer, or at the family altar in the morning. Then, for a few breaths, stop adding effort, and notice what's already here without making anything. If you don't pray, simply let the reward go.
Jnana. Knowing. On the fourth line, Shankara says freedom isn't produced by any action, so what frees is knowing what already is.
Your line: moksha isn't earned; it's what the self already is. Keep your horses, said the boy. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, good action and devotion are often understood as preparing the mind, while freedom itself is understood as coming through knowledge of the self.

Yama.meaning: Death, lord of the dead, Nachiketa's teacher

jnana.meaning: knowing, and the way of freedom through knowing

notes: Paraphrase of Shankara on 1.1.4: the force of 'tu' (but); the purvapaksha that the Upanishads serve injunctions; his reply that they teach Brahman as an existent; that what is produced is non-eternal; that release is not an effect of production, attainment, modification or purification. Confirm the fourfold list as stated and that it belongs to 1.1.4.

Shankara's view of action and devotion as preparing the mind (chitta-shuddhi) is stated briefly; confirm.
'Other Vedanta schools see freedom as given by the Lord's grace, met by devotion' summarizes Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita in one line; confirm it is fair.
